original.description: The ESA Antenna Laboratory operates several unique antenna and RF material measurement facilities, including the Sub-mmWave Scanner(SMS), LORENTZ cryogenic near-field scanner, and CATR Material Characterisation Facility. These facilities support antenna and RF characterisation activities covering a frequency range extending from microwave to sub-millimetre-wave frequencies and are routinely used in support of ESA programmes, technology developments, industrial activities and research campaigns.Operation ofthese facilities relies on dedicated custom-developed software that interfaces with motion control systems, network analysers and auxiliary equipment to perform automated measurements, collect measurement data and generate outputs suitable for post-processing andanalysis. Overthe past decade, this software has evolved through multiple development and maintenance activities, supporting successive laboratory upgrades and increasingly demanding measurement campaigns. The software currently comprises three principal application domains:            SMS scanner control software.            LORENTZ scanner control software.            CATR Material Characterisation control software.In addition, a growing set of shared software components has been introduced to provide common functionality across facilities, including hardware abstraction, configuration management, measurement orchestration, data management and graphical user interfaces. Historically, software development activities were executed through a number of independent projects. Consequently, different facilities evolved at different rates and software versions diverged over time. Recent maintenance activities have established a common software management approach based on GitLab repositories, issue tracking mechanisms and shared software components, improving traceability and maintainability of the software assets. The LORENTZ and CATR applications now share a modern architecture built around common software libraries and hardware abstraction layers. The SMS software remains operational but is based on anearlier architecture and represents the principal remaining source of technical debt within the software suite. Long-term sustainability of the Antenna Laboratory software therefore requires continued maintenance, harmonisation and progressive migration towards acommon software framework.The software environment further depends on several third-party components, including software drivers and interfaces fromKeysight, ACS Motion Control, Trio Motion Technology and other equipment suppliers. Maintaining compatibility withcommercial operating systems, hardware drivers and measurement instruments is therefore an essential part of maintaining the operational capability of the Antenna Laboratory. As several ESA facilities depend on the availability, reliability and traceability of measurement data,particular attention must be given to configuration control, software version management, measurement file compatibility and preservation of laboratory know-how. The software shall therefore be maintained as an operational laboratory asset rather than as a standalone development project.- Objective(s) of the ActivityThe objective of the activity is to ensure the continuous operation, maintenance, evolution and long-term sustainability of the Antenna Laboratory software systems, while preserving compatibility with existing facilities, measurement workflows and historical measurement data.

original.description: ESA operates one of the world's largest Earth Observation (EO) data archives, with data from missions dating back to the mid 1970s.Preserving these datatogether with the information and tools needed to interpret and use themis essential to analyse long-term environmental changes and support future decision-making. Within the EOF-EOS framework, long-term preservation of ESA's EO data holdings (Heritage Missions, Earth Explorers, Third Party Missions) and associated information and software is ensured through the Space Data Preservation System (SDPS), with assets located at ESRIN and external sites.Despite major progress, a significant volume of EO heritage data remains stored on legacy media at ESRIN and still requires transcription, recovery, and preservation in line with international standards. Beyond preservation and access, heritage data must be curated and improved to ensure continuity and comparability with newer missions. The generation of thematic collections and geographical datasets has further enhanced their usability and value.The Preservation Assets Operations and Maintenance (PAOM) Service will:Operate, maintain, and evolve Space Data Preservation System (SDPS) assets located at ESRIN;Manage the ESRIN EO Legacy Media Archive and Transcription Chains and perform legacy media transcription and data recovery;Generate thematic collections and geographical coverages using heritage data;Manage the ESRIN laboratory activities in support to transcription chains set-up and Philab Air Quality Platform activities, and manage and maintain the ESRIN AF Antenna;Support local visits at the Heritage Missions Walkthrough and Memorabilia Wall located at ESRIN and heritage missionsrelated outreach activities.

original.description: To derive more accurate expression of atmosphere irregularities effects with a focus on the ionosphere, and devise mitigation techniques for both geo- and sun-synchronous SAR imaging systemsDescription: For Low Earth Orbit (LEO) Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) systems the atmospheric turbulence is generally assumed to be time-invariant during the synthetic aperture time due to itsshort duration. Such assumption is not always correct, as horizontal atmospheric drifts and vortices exist. Especially for SAR systems at low frequency (P-Band, L-Band), SAR operating on repeat-track basis, geo-synchronous SAR systems characterised by long integration time and extensive imaging scene, the ionosphere can have an important role on the performance. Furthermore, both temporal andspatial variations of the ionosphere have to be jointly taken into account, which further complicates their characterisation. Therefore, the effects of the flowing ionospheric irregularities need to be investigated, aiming in particular to image shifts, defocusing and repeat-track interferometry. The aim of this activity is to provide a comprehensive analysis to evaluate effects of both spatial variation and flowing ionospheric irregularities on SAR systems operating both at P-, L- and C-band. In particular, the ionospheric scintillations, which act remarkably in the polar cap and equatorial zone at night need to be considered. The Ionosphere characterisation shall originate from previous developments, analyses performed in the framework of previous missions developments and from knowledge built up in the navigation community. This activity encompasses the following tasks: -Analytical models of the physical effects of spatial-temporally ionospheric background variations on the SAR signal. - Assessment of the impacts on the SAR performancesdemonstrating, both theoretically and numerically, the geometric fidelity, focusing aspect and interferometry quality (i.e., relative image shifts and the decorrelation of interferometric pairs, interferometric phase screen errors). - Validation of the models andof the performance analysis using ionospheric monitoring measurements (i.e., Global Positioning System). - Develop mitigation techniques. - The implementation of the aforementioned components in a software framework. The methods developed in this activity are expected to be developed in such a way that they can be later broadened to other atmospheric effects such as tropospheric scintillations. Software shall be delivered under an ESA Software Community License, so that any individuals or entities within ESA Member Statescan access to it and can provide update to the community of users.Deliverables: Report, SoftwareProcurement Policy: C(3) = Activity restricted to SMEs  RD  Entities. original.description: Objective: To derive a standard set of requirements for the ADHA (Advanced Data Handling Architecture) Security Module and implement a prototype form-factor equivalent ADHA module.Description: The ADHA (Advanced Data Handling Architecture) has been initiated through a collaboration between ESA, European satellite primes and data handling equipment suppliers. The initiative has resulted in the agreement on an architecture for data handling unit based on standard module functions. A standard module procurement flow has been defined, as well as a standardized backplane connector and electrical interfaces. This allows independent development of interoperable modules that can be connected together in ADHA units. More advanced security functions are expected to be required in future ESA missions. The modular format of the proposed solution will enable faster adoption, and verification of new security technologies, in different unit configurations. This activity aims to perform analysis work to derive a standardization of the security function within an ADHA module form-factor, to allow the development of ADHA-compliant security products, which can be utilized together with other existing ADHA products, such as ADHA OBC. When implemented in the ADHA 3U form factor, such units are of particular interest for use in mid-size satellite platforms as well (less than 500kg mass). For prototyping purposes, the target of this activity is an elegant breadboard (EBB) of the ADHA security module in 6U format, based on the security function requirements defined in this activity. The extended format will provide the required design margins for the prototyping and demonstration phase. The long-term goal, this technology development, is the adaptation of this security module to an ADHA 3U module form factor. This activity encompasses thefollowing tasks: - Analyse the use-cases for dedicated security modules in data handling systems, both for platform and payload - Derive the detailed generic requirements for ADHA Security Modules, including functions, performances, electrical and software interfaces, etc. and present the specifications for review of the ADHA consortia and industrial working group - Derive the architectural design of a prototype ADHA Security Module - Derive a prototype electrical and software design of an ADHA Security Module, as an EBB in ADHA 6U format. - Perform functional validation of the prototype and demonstrate a representative use-case for the ADHA Security Module - Derive a roadmap for bringing the derived design to an ADHA 3U security module EM/EQM/FM.

original.description: Objective: The objective of the activity is to design, develop and test a 1 Gbit/s DVB-S2/S2X demodulator and 500 Mbit/s multi-frequency TDMA modulator on a high performance x86, ARM, or similar CPU based Commercial-off-the-Shelf (COTS) platforms.Targeted Improvements: 10-fold data rate increase compared to existing full DVB standards-compliant software defined radio implementations.Description: Current software-defined modems have demonstrated throughputs of around 100 Mbit/s, with some claims of significantlyhigher performance using specialised hardware and limiting the demodulator to one modcod only. Conversely, a high-performance modemrunning on a generic CPU platform opens up the possibility to deploy field-upgradable modems on server hardware for professional and governmental applications.This activity will study the implementation of DVB-S2 and S2X compliant demodulation algorithms as well as DVB-RCS2 MF-TDMA compliant modulation algorithms on high performance x86, ARM, or similar CPU based Commercial-off-the-Shelf (COTS) platforms. A CPU-based software-defined radio with a throughput of 1 Gbit/s in DVB-S2X and 500 Mbit/s in MF-TDMA will be designedand developed.
